pages.name: Star: where you measure
pages.text: Three windings a third of a turn apart make three voltages 120° apart, 230 V each. The supply is in [[star]]: one end of every winding meets at the star point, and lines L1, L2 and L3 run from the free ends to three loads, joined the same way. Across one winding the voltmeter reads the [[phase voltage]], 230 V. Between L1 and L2 it reads L1's arrow minus L2's, √3, about 1.732, times as long: 230 × 1.732 = 398.4 V, the [[line voltage]].

pages.name: Between two lines
pages.task: Say a supply makes 254 V a winding, in star. What does the voltmeter between L1 and L2 read?
pages.why: Going from L2 to L1 you pass back down L2's winding and up L1's, so the meter reads L1's arrow minus L2's. To take an arrow away, turn it half round and add it. L2's arrow, turned round, sits on the tip of L1's, and the arrow closing them is √3, about 1.732, times as long, turned 30° from L1's. So 254 × 1.732 = 439.9 V, about 440 V, the line voltage most ships run. 508 V adds the two as plain numbers, as if they peaked together.

pages.name: Star: the currents
pages.text: Now the currents. Each line runs straight into one winding and one load, with nothing branching off, so the [[line current]] is the phase current. Each load is 23 Ω at a power factor of 0.8, so each phase carries 230 ÷ 23 = 10 A, 36.9° behind its own voltage. At the star point the three currents meet and go back along the [[neutral]], which carries all three added as arrows.

pages.name: The neutral
pages.task: Three 10 A phase currents meet at the star point. What does the neutral carry?
pages.why: Laid tip to tail, three equal arrows 120° apart close a triangle. The last tip lands back on the first tail, so their sum is nothing: at every instant, what flows out along one line flows back along the other two. A balanced load leaves the neutral carrying nothing, so a load that is always balanced can be fed by the three lines alone. Most ships' main supply is just that: three phases on three wires, with no neutral conductor.

pages.name: Unbalance
pages.text: The slider is yours now: L3's load current. L1 and L2 stay at 10 A. As L3 falls, the triangle stops closing and the neutral's arrow grows across the gap. Each phase still shares an equal part, L3's current, which cancels as before. What is left is L1's and L2's extra, two equal arrows 120° apart, whose sum is one arrow just as long. So the neutral carries 10 A minus L3's current: 4 A with L3 at 6 A, and 10 A with L3 off.

pages.name: 10, 10 and 7
pages.task: L1 and L2 carry 10 A, and L3 carries 7 A. What does the neutral carry?
pages.why: The equal part, 7 A in each phase, closes a triangle and cancels. What is left is L1's and L2's extra 3 A, two equal arrows 120° apart, whose sum is one 3 A arrow. So the neutral carries 3 A, not 27 A. That cancelling holds for sine-wave currents; currents with harmonics at three times the supply frequency add in the neutral instead.

pages.name: Delta
pages.text: The switch now joins the same loads in [[delta]]. The supply stays in star, so from here phase means one load. Each load sits between two lines, in a ring, with no star point and no neutral, so it has the line voltage across it, 398.4 V, and draws 398.4 ÷ 23 = 17.32 A. At L1's corner, L1 brings the current of the load that starts there, less the current the other load delivers back. That is the difference of two phase currents 120° apart, the same subtraction as before, now on the currents: 17.32 × 1.732 = 30.0 A.

pages.name: Delta: the line current
pages.task: Other loads in delta each draw 12 A. What does the clamp on L1 read?
pages.why: L1's corner joins two loads. L1 brings the current of the load that starts there, less the current of the load that ends there: two 12 A phase currents 120° apart. Turn the second half round and lay it on the tip of the first, and the arrow closing them is √3 times as long, 12 × 1.732 = 20.8 A. The √3 has moved from the voltage to the current. 24 A adds them as plain numbers, as if they peaked together.

pages.name: Power, either way
pages.text: Each load takes V_ph × I_ph × cos φ, lesson 8's true power, so three take 3 × V_ph × I_ph × cos φ. In star, V_ph = V_L ÷ √3 and I_ph = I_L. In delta, V_ph = V_L and I_ph = I_L ÷ √3. Either way one √3 divides into the 3 and leaves √3 × V_L × I_L × cos φ, so the two readouts always agree. Flip the switch and watch both: 5520 W in star, 16,561 W in delta.

pages.name: Heaters, star to delta
pages.task: Three heaters take 1725 W in star, 2.5 A each. Joined in delta on the same supply, what do they take?
pages.why: In delta each heater has √3 times the voltage across it, 398.4 V instead of 230 V, so it draws √3 times the current, 4.33 A instead of 2.5 A. Its power goes with both, so it rises √3 × √3 = 3 times: 3 × 1725 = 5175 W. Fixed loads such as heaters, moved from star to delta on the same supply, take three times the power.

pages.name: Mixed: a board
pages.task: Mixed. A board reads 400 V between lines. A balanced load draws 20 A a line at a power factor of 0.85, and you cannot see how it is joined. What apparent power, in volt-amps, do its cables carry?
pages.why: Apparent power is volts times amps with the angle left out, lesson 8's volt-amps. With line values, three phases' worth is √3 × V_L × I_L, whatever the connection: √3 × 400 × 20 = 13,856 VA, about 13.9 kVA. Only the cos φ share arrives as watts: 13,856 × 0.85 = 11,778 W, about 11.8 kW.

pages.task: Mixed. A motor's windings are joined in delta, and the clamp reads 26 A on one line. What current flows in each winding?
pages.why: In delta each line joins two windings and carries the difference of their currents, √3 times one of them. So each winding carries the line current ÷ √3: 26 ÷ 1.732 = 15.0 A. Two 15.0 A arrows 120° apart differ by an arrow 26 A long.

pages.name: Mixed: the peak
pages.task: Mixed. The meter reads 400 V between two lines. Like the 230 V on a label, that is rms. What peak voltage does the insulation between them see?
pages.why: 400 V is rms, as lesson 2 showed for the 230 V label, and a sine peaks at √2, about 1.414, times its rms: 400 × 1.414 = 566 V. The connection does not matter here. √3 goes from phase to line; √2 goes from rms to peak. Choose the tool by what you are changing.
